We need to question him, possibly arrest him"? Did he ever say that to you or to the other police officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether he would say that to other colleagues, but he never said that to me, and I have never heard anything to that effect from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go back to the 22nd of June and ask you: Did you recognise anyone else there, aside from VG117?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: No, I didn't quite understand your question, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you've told us that you recognised VG117 there. Out of this group of a hundred people, can you tell us who else you recognised there at the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: On no occasion did I say that I had recognised a person that we call VG117.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that you did not see VG117 at the school on the 22nd of June?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: Yes. I am testifying that I didn't see her, I didn't recognise her, nor that she was there. In any case, I didn't see her there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'd ask you just to look down at the sheet in front of you again to make sure we're not confusing two different people. It's VG117 -- I'm sorry. VG117. Is it your testimony you did not see her at the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: Well, I said earlier on that I hadn't seen her personally but that I found out that she was there because she was supposed to have gone to Serbia by car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who told you that she was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: Djuric and Ristic, the soldiers of the Territorial Defence. They told me that there were some people there that were to be taken to Serbia and to be taken over by a high-ranking officer in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's quite possible that VG117 may have arrived at the school after you had left the school; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: She arrived along with the other people from the villages I mentioned. She wasn't in the trucks, but she was driven in a Lada Niva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the group at the school was mostly made up of elderly people, women and children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: Yes. Most of them were elderly people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe you told us that the people remained at the school for three to four days. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: Well, they stayed for more days; seven, eight, or nine days. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, were there any -- was there any place for the people to get food at the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, whether they received food at the school, but they could go to the shops, to their relatives living in town, or to Serbs, to their neighbour Serbs whom they knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the reasons you told us that they were at the school for this period of time was because it was too dangerous to take them back to the village of Gostilja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: That is correct. There were attempts to return to Gostilja, but the Muslims from the left bank of the Drina were firing and it was not possible for them to reach the places where they resided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the only road that you could go back or return to Gostilja, would that be the road that runs along the Drina? Was that the only way back to Gostilja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. The only road communications which could be used by cars, by vehicles, was the one on the right bank of the Drina River, and the Muslims were on the left bank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, can you explain to us, then, if it's too dangerous to take these people back along that road to their village, how was it not too dangerous for the Lada Niva to drive with VG117 to Gostilja, to stay at the house of Mr. Joksimovic? How is that not too dangerous?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: Those people, when they were taken by truck to return to the village of Gostilja, I repeat that the Muslims were shooting from the left bank of the Drina, and therefore, to avoid casualties, these people were returned to the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how could you be sure that the Muslims would not shoot at the Lada Niva as it drove along the same road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't sure. The Lada is smaller in size and it's more difficult to hit than a larger freight vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the people, if they were permitted to, could have walked through the hills to Gostilja from the Vuk Karadzic school without ever going near the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: At no moment were these people prevented from coming or going. Where they were at school, in the school building, they went to their relatives who were Muslims or in the neighbourhood to Serbs. Their freedom of movement was in no way restricted at any moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to return to Milena Pencencic. You recognised the last name, you were unsure about her first name. Isn't it a fact that prior to the people of Gostilja being brought into Visegrad, that you and approximately 15 other men, dressed in -- with the uniform you've described or with balaclavas covering your faces, that you went to that village shooting before you got into that village and that you disarmed that village, and in fact took a young man who was an SDA member and threatened him and threatened to burn down the village if the people there did not turn over any weapons that they have? Is that not a fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: No, never. I had never occasion, while the war was waging, to be in the village of Gostilja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever conduct searches for weapons in Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: No, never did I have occasion to search for weapons. These were not my orders, the orders I received from my superiors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my last question to you is: Isn't it a fact that, prior to you agreeing to come to testify before this Chamber, you required some guarantee that you would not be arrested or charged with a crime while you were here? Is that not true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: No, I did not ask for such protection. Probably the Defence counsel of Mitar Vasiljevic asked for that. Well, I only asked for facial distortions because I have to move around the Federation and I don't want to have any trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet. Re-examined by Mr. Domazet:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of Mr. Groome's questions was whether anyone from the Red Cross came and wrote names down. In any situation, did you ever see people from the Red Cross coming to record the names of the people who were preparing to join the convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: I never had occasion to see that. I have never seen people to come to record the names of people who were to travel in a convoy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Please remember, sir, that you are speaking the same language as Mr. Domazet, so pause before your answer begins so that the interpreters can catch up; otherwise, we lose some of your answer, and we do want to hear everything you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were answering Mr. Groome's question about whether you personally could confuse the identity of Zilic Stanimir and Mitar Vasiljevic, you spoke about general examples how this can happen, but in the case of these two people, there was a very specific question. Do you know both of them very well, and is that why you said that you could not be mistaken about them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: It is true what I stated. I know both persons very well and I could not mistake one for the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judging by the characteristics that you have mentioned, can you say that these people look alike, and within the framework of what you have said, would this change anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: I just said that they had things in common, like same hair colouring, same complexion and build.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were answering the question about people that were taken to the police station without ID papers, without being able to keep them there, you said that these people -- you were asked whether these people could have been taken to prison. Could you tell me whether a prison existed in Visegrad before that or after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: A prison always existed as a premise, but no one was taken there to be arrested there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which premises are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: I'm referring to the premise which every police station in the former Yugoslavia had to detain people. But during that time, people did not bring other people there to keep them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understood that. Every police station has a room where it keeps, it detains people for a certain period of time, and it is entitled to do so, but this is restricted, the time is restricted.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: Yes, this is restricted in time, and as the international policemen are here, and according to the new laws, the people cannot be kept there without the consent of the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my question does not refer to the premises in a police station where you can detain someone for some period of time. My question was whether the town of Visegrad had a prison. You're a policeman, you know what a prison is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: Well, Visegrad as such did not have any prison, only in the barracks there, there was a number of people who were captured and they waited -- they were awaiting to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of Mr. Groome's questions was whether you saw members of the Milan Lukic group. You said that you had seen them, that they were armed. Amongst those that you saw, did you recognise any people from Visegrad, and were the people belonging to his group, were they people from Visegrad, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: Aside from Milan Lukic, all other people were unknown to me, and they were not from the territory of Visegrad, these were people from Serbia. I don't know exactly from where, but they were not from the areas of Visegrad, nor the town of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of Mr. Groome's questions was how come there was a danger to the people who were being transported from the school to Gostilja and that such a danger did not exist for the Lada Niva vehicle. And in connection with that, I ask you: To the best of your knowledge, was there a danger for the trucks passing by or was there actual shooting and that was the reason why they returned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: I didn't say that there was only a danger, but there was actual shooting going on, firing at the trucks that wished to return these people to the location mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, the witness has taken no notice of me, but he may take some notice of you if you just ask him, please, to pause before he starts his answer. It's making it terribly difficult for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm just in the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of Mr. Groome's questions was whether the people from that school you mentioned, whether they could reach Gostilja on foot, because you said that the only communication line was along the Drina River. You said that they were not prevented from doing so and that they could do so. I think that was your answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: That is correct. The only road for vehicles was along the Drina River; but on foot, they could reach Gostilja in different -- in a number of different ways.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who returned to this school and remained there as long as they said, you said that they went in different directions. Do you know whether these people returned to Gostilja on foot or not, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: Well, to the best of my knowledge, I know that some of them went to Serbia, some went via Gostilja to Zepa, through the village where I was born.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Only one last question. Well, you said what you knew about the Red Cross, who was employed there and where the Red Cross was located. Is the Red Cross still located there where it was located in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD24
utterances.text: The Red Cross premises are now located elsewhere, because that building, in fact, the building next to it, the restaurant next to it, was mined, and due to the explosion, the Red Cross building was also damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for coming to give evidence and for the evidence which you have given. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my last witness is the accused, Mitar Vasiljevic, in connection with the Vuk Karadzic incident and his acquaintance with VG117.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. Let's have Mr. Vasiljevic in the witness box, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vasiljevic, you understand, do you, you are still bound by the solemn declaration which you gave when you first gave evidence before us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You don't need to stand up; you can stay seated. Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Domazet:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, I have a couple of questions for you concerning what we have heard from VG117. Do you remember what individual I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And please bear in mind that you must not mention her name.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We're just placing one of those pseudonym sheets in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, if you remember, VG117 first spoke about her childhood, and she told us that she minded the cattle when she was young and played with the children from neighbouring villages. Among others, she also mentioned yourself and your village. Do you know anything about that? Do you have any recollection of that, and is there anything that you can tell us about what you did and where you were at that time, what property you had and did you also, from time to time, take care of the cattle

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: I know exactly where Muslim property lies. It was at a considerable distance from our property. Muslim and Serb properties were quite apart, if you go from the Drina River. The Muslim property would be situated further up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you surely know your properties, that is, where your father's property is, and you also know where the so-called Muslim property begins. Are you referring to the people from the same village that she comes from? And how is it that you know that this is Muslim property?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: The village of VG117 is located there, and I know that the property of those villagers belongs below -- begins below the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Notwithstanding the distance of this property, do you remember your childhood? Did you also from time to time mind the cattle? Did you play with the children from neighbouring villages, including the village where VG117 was born and lived as a child?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: I went to school in the village of VG117. She is not exactly from that particular village. She comes from a small hamlet situated one kilometre away from the school, but I didn't pass through that hamlet on my way to school. However, I do know people from that village, children from that village who went to school with me, but I didn't know her, because she is six years my senior, so I could not have played with her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you couldn't play with her, was it because of the difference in age, the six-year difference being considerable for that age group?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: We didn't go to school together, and then -- well, I was what, 7 when I went to school. She was 13. We belonged to two different generations, I mean. I was a small child, like I said. When I started going to school, she had already completed four years of schooling, if we're speaking about the same school in which I went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you trying to tell us that it was impossible for you to have seen her at that school because the school had only four classes, four forms, four generations, and she had already left by the time you went to school?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VG117, in her testimony, mentioned a couple of boys belonging to her generation but who were from your village, if you remember that, and she couldn't remember any other name except for yours, and I'm referring to the names of children not belonging to her generation. Do you know the persons whom she mentioned as being of the same generation as she is?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: I know all individuals she mentioned. They're all my neighbours. As for Bozo Kovacevic, he's not Kovacevic, he's Markovic. But I know them all, although they are older. They went to school with her, not with me. I don't remember -- I don't remember her from school. I was 5 years old by the time they completed the fourth form.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The three individuals that she mentioned and that you know, except that she made a mistake with the surname of one of them, are familiar to you; you know them. Did you ever play with them when you were a boy?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, never. They are older than me. They did not belong to the same generation. There were 39 of us who went to the school in the village of VG117. There were 39 of us in my generation. I mean, some went to the first form, some to the second, the third or the fourth, but we were 39, that is, the people who were at that school at the same time I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one last question concerning this particular issue, Mr. Vasiljevic: You spoke about the property of your father and the property of these other families as being quite apart. Could you approximate for us the distance, either in kilometres or in time, that you would need to walk from one property to another?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, the way she explained, I don't think it was possible for me to have minded cattle when I was 7. I was already at school. And before that, I was much too young. I would have had to have someone older with me. I could not have been a very reliable shepherd. It was an open area and it was prohibited to walk around the cattle wherever you wanted. It was simply not possible for me to have done that at that time. I'm much younger than she is. She fabricated all of that. Their property is at a considerable distance from ours. I would have needed at least 20 minutes on foot to reach her property, though exactly I don't know where that property is located. I just have an idea of it. We're talking about rather large properties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, when you say that you would need at least 20 minutes to reach the property on foot, are you referring to the first Muslim farms or the one that actually belonged to that family?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't know where exactly their farm, their property is. I just know where these properties are all together. Like I said, I went to school to this Muslim village. The school had only four classes, four forms. And somewhere halfway to the school, Muslim properties began. So first I would have to cross Serb properties, and then the second half would be the Muslim properties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you remember, Mr. Vasiljevic, Witness 117 then went on and spoke about that, in addition to the fact that she knew you when she was a child, she often saw you working as a waiter in Visegrad and that you sometimes waited on her at the Panos restaurant and the restaurant belonging to the Vilina Vlas hotel. I should now like to ask several questions concerning the time that you spent working as a waiter. To the best of your recollection, how many waiters were there working in your company in Visegrad at that time?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: The number varied, in particular, in summer, when seasonal workers were employed. I don't know; 50, 60 to 70, and probably more in summertime. We were one of the largest companies there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the figure that you mentioned. Because I don't think the record reflects what you said accurately. Would you please repeat the number of waiters working at that time, to the best of your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Between 65 and 70, and in summertime probably more. Between 65 and 70 waiters altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That is indeed what you said initially, but the record did not reflect that. I just want to make it clear for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, one of the reasons the record may have been incorrect is that your client, I'm afraid, is not pausing before he gives his answer, and he is starting his answer whilst the interpreters are still translating your question. Perhaps you might remind him to pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I think I was doing my best. Maybe I did speed up a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, would you please pause between you starting to answer my question, in order to avoid mistakes in the transcript. As regards your colleagues, the waiters whose number you mentioned, do you remember if there were any waiters coming from the village of Gostilja, where VG117 lived?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, three of my colleagues were VG117's neighbours. They worked with me for a long time. She did not mention them. She failed to mention them but they are from her village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know their names, and if so, could you tell us their names?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. I know all three of them. Ismet Murtic, Milorad Joksimovic, and Nenad Andric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness VG117 testified that she had been a client of yours in two specific restaurants: Panos and Vilina Vlas hotel. Did you work in these restaurants, and if so, when, according to what you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: The Panos restaurant belonged to my company, the Panos company, and I used to work there for - I couldn't tell you exactly - for maybe seven or -- it was seven or eight years prior to the war that I didn't work there. I worked at the Visegrad hotel. However, while I was younger -- in this Panos restaurant, it is a town restaurant. It was usually older waiters that worked there. And in wintertime, when we had no work at the Visegrad hotel, we would either replace them when they were on leave or for some other reasons, but it was mostly in wintertime that we worked there. So I did work at the Panos restaurant on a couple of occasions, I don't know exactly how many. As for Vilina Vlas, I was never fully employed there, that is, permanently. The facility was part of our company shortly after it had been built, but very soon it was transferred to another company, to the local recreational centre and spa. And those people who were employed there at the time were also transferred, they were also there, but we remained with the Panos restaurant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly when you said that, according to your recollection, during the seven or eight years preceding the war you did not work at the Panos restaurant?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't know how precise that is, but thereabouts. I know that I didn't work there for several years prior to the war. How many, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which restaurant did you work prior to the outbreak of conflict, that is, before the spring 1992?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: At the Visegrad hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember how much time before the spring of 1992 you spent working at the Visegrad hotel?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: I think I worked there up until March, thereabouts. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you want to say is that you worked there until March 1992. I'm asking you about the time before that. How much time before that, how many years or months did you work at the Visegrad hotel at all times, that is, without interruption?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. I worked there without any break, but I don't know exactly how long. Perhaps for seven or eight years. But let me explain something. We didn't go to the Panos restaurant to replace workers who were on leave only. There were other restaurants; a Mezalin, Bruga [phoen]. We waiters from the Visegrad hotel would often go to replace our colleagues elsewhere, because we were not that many during wintertime. It was not necessary for so many of us to be permanently at the Visegrad hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think I understand your answer. However, I think it would be advisable to add some clarification to it. Does it mean that you spent seven or eight years prior to the war working at the Visegrad hotel; however, during winter months, because terraces were closed, from time to time you would be replacing your colleagues, waiters in other catering establishments, who were on leave, who were on holiday? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: I cannot be specific. I cannot tell you exactly in which restaurant, in which year, and so on and so forth, and who it was that I was replacing at that time. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, before I ask you specific questions concerning VG117, let me ask you something else. Since you spent your entire working life working as a waiter and working in various cafes and other catering establishments, how customary was it for women to go alone and have a cup of coffee, a drink, or dinner in one of such establishments?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Not very often. I mean, very seldom did we have such women guests, especially at the Panos restaurant, and in other cafes in town very rarely did we have women who were alone, visiting the cafe. But, I mean, they did from time to time. I'm not saying that it never happened, but it was a very rare occurrence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In cases of such visits by lone women, would it be normal for you to remember something like that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: I'm not trying to say that I never waited on VG117. That wouldn't be fair, because I waited on hundreds of people. However, I don't remember her as a guest, especially in view of what she told us, that she was a very frequent guest of such establishments. We all know what a frequent guest is, what a regular customer is. I didn't know her as such. We are all familiar with our regulars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You probably remember, Mr. Vasiljevic, how she told us that she would go to the Panos restaurant because it was situated close to the market, and sometimes she went to the market to sell her goods there, and, after that, she would go to that restaurant to have lunch. To your recollection, did you have such customers in Panos when you were there? Because you told us that from time to time you worked there. Was it customary for people who came to the market to sell their own products to come to your restaurant to have a meal after they had finished? Did you observe that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: I remember that she said that, but I don't remember waiting on anyone who was from the market. I mean, people who had just sold one kilo or two kilos of some local produce, cheese or so, to come to the restaurant and have a meal there, I don't remember that. I'm not saying I never waited on her. Maybe I know her, but again, it's ... Like I said, I cannot say that I never waited on her. I spent, after all, 17 years working as a waiter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't quite understand what you said about your sister. Did your sister also come to the market? Where did she live? Did she also sell local produce to the market, and did she go to the restaurant to have a meal?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: My brother-in-law was into farming. He was a farmer and he was -- he went to the market on Wednesdays. Every Wednesday, he would be on the market, and I never waited on my sister, no. It's quite expensive for a farmer who sells his goods at the market to go to a restaurant and have a meal there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That would have been my next question. You are familiar with the circumstances and life in general at that time. People who sold their own products at the market, could they afford to have a meal at your restaurant, according to your assessment?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, of course not. Many of those people went to the market on foot. They couldn't even afford to have some other kind of transportation to go to the market. They would cover kilometres on foot, and it's especially those people who come to the market to sell their own goods who are very, very frugal, very careful about how they spend their money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, when you said that you weren't clear or you didn't understand what he had said about your sister, I heard nothing about his sister. What did you hear him say about his sister?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm afraid I was not looking at the transcript. I don't know whether the interpretation in question included the sister. But before I asked the question, he said that her sister too [sic] had come to the market but that he had never waited on her as a waiter in that restaurant. And that was -- I think that he answered my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He certainly answered that when you raised the issue, but I'm only concerned that we may have missed something. I don't know whether it's important or not. But there is no record in the transcript, that I can see, that he had ever mentioned his sister before you asked the question, when you said you had not understood what he had said about her. Now, if it was not important, let's proceed, but if it was important, you had better get it recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm sure that he did mention sister, and that was the reason for the question that followed, but I don't think that it is of any crucial importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me now move on to the second part of the testimony of VG117, when she declared that on the 22nd of June, 1992, she saw you in front of the Vuk Karadzic school, that is, that she saw you coming and sitting at a desk, making a record of something.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, I also testified before this Honourable Chamber that I had gone to hospital on the 14th of June, 1992, and she simply could not have seen that. It was not possible for her to see me, though she testified that she had seen me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your opinion that she knew you sufficiently well as to be able to recognise you as Mitar Vasiljevic, the waiter?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that I knew her husband. However, I never knew that VG117 was his wife, never. But I know the husband, mostly because it was with his brother, the officer who has been mentioned here, is one of my school colleagues. I went to school with him, although I think he was one or two years older than me. Maybe two. Yes, I think he's two years older than me. And I know that he liked to drink. He would keep his uniform on. He used to work as a janitor in a company, and he would keep his uniform on. I knew him, but I never know the fact that VG was his wife, until she testified that. Now I know. Now I know who her husband is. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I think we're coming to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There's just one question I'd like to have -- I can probably find it if I look for long enough, but what year was your client born in?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think in 1954.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is that what the evidence is or is that your interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is in the indictment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Now, we'll have to adjourn now, but we have managed to obtain a courtroom in the morning, so we don't have to sit through tomorrow afternoon, I hope. How long do you think you'll be with the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think no longer than 15 minutes or 20 minutes, no more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And without trying to tie you down, Mr. Groome, how long do you think you'll be?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think very briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Okay. That means we should surely finish tomorrow morning. We'll be in courtroom 3. We'll start at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: 10.00 tomorrow. We'll adjourn until then.
